overview: This file brings together U.S. diplomatic reporting on the Japanese press from December 1938 through February 1939. The first portion consists of Nagoya consular reports and translated newspaper items documenting Japan’s wartime mobilization: accelerated engineering and aviation education, regulated rubber prices, revived exports to occupied China, expansion and consolidation of military industries, and attempts to address overwork, illness, housing shortages, and nutrition among munitions workers. The final telegrams shift to international affairs, reporting Japanese press claims that the United States was abandoning isolation, cooperating with Britain and France, fortifying Guam, protesting Japan’s occupation of Hainan, and contemplating financial measures against Japan, Germany, and Italy in South America; the Department of State replied by referring the embassy to an official statement concerning the Export-Import Bank.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of four recent Nagoya press items
subfiles.from: Charles H. Stephan, American Vice Consul at Nagoya
subfiles.to: Joseph Clark Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Stephan forwards four translations concerning productive capacity, aviation education, rubber quotations, and Nagoya’s exports to China.
subfiles.summary: The vice consul presents four local press items bearing on Japan’s operations in China. They address the rapid training of engineers, creation of an aviation department at Nagoya Technological College, official crude-rubber prices, and the reported recovery of Nagoya’s China trade in November 1938. Copies were distributed to the embassy, the Tokyo consulate general, and the Department of State.

subfiles.title: Training engineers and expanding technical education
subfiles.to: U.S. Embassy, Tokyo, as an enclosure from the American Consulate at Nagoya
subfiles.about: The article describes a national program to train engineers quickly and establish new aviation and engineering departments in Nagoya.
subfiles.summary: The Department of Education reportedly planned to mobilize educational institutions to increase Japan’s productive capacity during the prolonged war in China. The proposed appropriation was ¥5.7 million for the coming fiscal year. It included a new aviation department at Nagoya Technological College and an engineering department at the proposed Nagoya Imperial University.

subfiles.title: Aviation Department at Nagoya Technological College
subfiles.to: U.S. Embassy, Tokyo, as an enclosure from the American Consulate at Nagoya
subfiles.about: The article announces plans to open an aviation department at Nagoya Technological College in early 1939.
subfiles.summary: Funding for the long-awaited aviation department had reportedly been placed in the Department of Education’s estimates. The department was expected initially to enroll forty students. The college had begun making provisional arrangements for classrooms and dormitory accommodations.

subfiles.title: Official crude-rubber quotations in Aichi
subfiles.to: U.S. Embassy, Tokyo, as an enclosure from the American Consulate at Nagoya
subfiles.about: The enclosure records official maximum prices for several classes and origins of crude rubber.
subfiles.summary: The Aichi Chemical Products Price Adjusting Committee submitted crude-rubber quotations to the prefectural authorities, with prices said to match those in the Tokyo district. The table covers rubber designated Batavia “E,” Singapore No. 2, Makassar “C,” and large and small Congo grades, along with their containers and prices per kin. It also supplies a pound conversion and the current yen-dollar exchange rate.

subfiles.title: Recovery of Nagoya’s exports to China
subfiles.to: U.S. Embassy, Tokyo, as an enclosure from the American Consulate at Nagoya
subfiles.about: The article claims that Nagoya’s export trade with China recovered dramatically after the fall of Hankou.
subfiles.summary: Nagoya Customs reported November exports to China worth ¥1.522 million, compared with ¥81,000 in August 1937. The paper attributed the recovery to the fall of Hankou and reconstruction measures in Japanese-occupied Chinese territory. It also reported 120 regular and irregular vessel runs carrying flour, woolens, beer, machinery, and hardware from Nagoya to China.

subfiles.title: Transmittal on military industries and labor in Nagoya
subfiles.from: Charles H. Stephan, American Vice Consul at Nagoya
subfiles.to: Joseph Clark Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Stephan forwards two press translations on the expansion of Nagoya’s military industries and mounting labor problems.
subfiles.summary: The report introduces two local newspaper items. One concerns the rapid wartime expansion of Nagoya’s heavy and military industries during 1938. The other addresses worker absenteeism caused by overwork, illness, poor housing, and unsatisfactory living conditions.

subfiles.title: Rapid growth and consolidation of Nagoya industries
subfiles.to: U.S. Embassy, Tokyo, as an enclosure from the American Consulate at Nagoya
subfiles.about: The article reports capital growth, new enterprises, dissolutions, and consolidation among Nagoya’s wartime industries.
subfiles.summary: A Nagoya City Office investigation found that authorized capital among companies operating in the city had reached ¥845 million by October 31, 1938, an increase of more than ¥125 million since January. Much of the increase came from firms producing aircraft, vehicles, railway equipment, machinery, munitions, and military supplies. Although 211 companies had been established, 330 were dissolved, many through mergers or absorption in accordance with national industrial policy.

subfiles.title: Organization of the Aichi War-Labor Control Committee
subfiles.to: U.S. Embassy, Tokyo, as an enclosure from the American Consulate at Nagoya
subfiles.about: The article describes a new committee intended to stabilize munitions labor by addressing illness, overwork, housing, and nutrition.
subfiles.summary: Aichi Prefecture established a War-Labor Control Committee under Governor Tanaka to sustain production of munitions and military supplies. Authorities were concerned by rising illness-related absenteeism attributed to overwork and inadequate living conditions, especially the difficulty low-paid workers faced in finding affordable housing. Proposed remedies included small houses and communal dining facilities offering nutritious food. The article lists military, police, governmental, commercial, and industrial leaders appointed to the committee.

subfiles.title: Grew telegram on Japanese press interpretations of U.S. policy
subfiles.from: Joseph Clark Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Grew reports Japanese press claims that the United States was aligning with Britain and France and planning financial pressure against Japan and the other Axis powers.
subfiles.summary: Japanese newspapers interpreted American debates over aircraft sales, naval expansion, and fortifying Guam as evidence that the United States was abandoning isolation and aligning itself with Britain and France. They likewise portrayed American representations concerning Japan’s occupation of Hainan as part of coordinated action by the three powers. Grew also summarized an Asahi dispatch alleging that Washington intended to use loans and manufacturing subsidies to close South American markets to Japan, Germany, and Italy and restrict their access to foreign exchange and raw materials. The dispatch connected this purported policy to the resignation of Assistant Treasury Secretary Taylor.

subfiles.title: Hull reply concerning the Export-Import Bank charter
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull, U.S. Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Hull directs the embassy to an official letter concerning the proposed extension of the Export-Import Bank’s charter.
subfiles.summary: The Department responds specifically to the second numbered paragraph of Grew’s February 21 telegram. Hull notes that Radio Bulletin No. 43 reproduced a letter from the Secretary of State to the chairman of the Reconstruction Finance Corporation concerning extension of the Export-Import Bank of Washington’s charter. The brief reply evidently supplied official context for the Japanese press allegations about American financial diplomacy.

interest: The file is valuable because it links detailed local evidence of Japan’s wartime economic mobilization with broader Japanese perceptions of an emerging anti-Axis alignment abroad. The Nagoya enclosures contain unusually specific quantitative evidence—capital totals, commodity prices, export figures, shipping frequency, and proposed student enrollment—along with a roster connecting military authorities, police, prefectural officials, and major industrial firms. The labor committee article is especially useful for showing how overwork, illness, housing scarcity, and nutrition threatened military production. The later telegrams reveal how Japanese newspapers framed American rearmament and financial policy as coordinated strategic pressure well before the outbreak of the Pacific War.
